title: The mobile visit for an independent school
metaTitle: The mobile visit for an independent school
excerpt: Parents will judge the school on a phone. The first screen has to show students in the day and a way to visit or inquire, not a shrunken crest.
alt: Two white smartwatch mockups on a plain light background, one showing the face and one the back, small screens that still have to carry one clear fact.
caption: A small screen has room for one clear fact. A school homepage should spend it on the day. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should the first phone screen contain?
faqs.answer: A photograph of students at work, one sentence with the age and a true limit or advantage, and a visit or inquiry control. Do not open on a crest or a mission line. Design this screen on its own. Do not crop the desktop prospectus and hope.

faqs.question: How large should the visit control be?
faqs.answer: Tall enough for a thumb, separate from the menu, and quick to respond. If a year is full, say so beside the control. Keep the word visit consistent with the header so a parent who switches devices does not have to relearn the path.

faqs.question: How do you check the page?
faqs.answer: Load it cold on a phone that is not the design monitor, in daylight, and complete a visit request with a thumb. web.dev's good thresholds are largest contentful paint within 2.5 seconds, a tap response within 200 milliseconds, and layout shift of 0.1 or less. Then ask a parent to find the end of the school day without help.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
An independent school mobile website is where most parents will make the comparison. The first screen still has to show students and the day, not a crest, and offer a way to visit or inquire. Do not let the desktop prospectus decide the phone page. The phone is the page they will believe.

Nielsen Norman Group's research puts a hard edge on that first screen. People often leave within 10 to 20 seconds, and the offer has to be clear inside the first 10 if you want any longer attention. web.dev's Core Web Vitals say what the screen costs to deliver. Largest Contentful Paint within 2.5 seconds, Interaction to Next Paint at 200 milliseconds or less, and Cumulative Layout Shift at 0.1 or less. A parent on a pavement outside the gate is where those numbers stop being abstract.

## The phone is the comparison

Assume the parent is slightly distracted, with two other schools in adjacent tabs, often one-handed, sometimes with the child beside them. They are not at a board table admiring a wide layout. They are trying to decide whether a visit is worth a Saturday.

Design for that posture first. The day and the visit have to fit in the opening view without a pinch and without a scroll that feels like a gamble. If the desktop design is a full-viewport crest with a mission line and a tiny arrow, the phone inherits a crop of a shield and a sentence too small to read. Throw that composition out. You may keep a wide version only if it still shows students. Often the honest move is to change both.

Read the first screen from the phone, out loud, in daylight. The words have to be large enough that nobody zooms. Zooming means the type was chosen on a monitor for a print-like brochure. Increase it until the sentence about the day fits and remains a sentence.

The other schools are one gesture away. You do not get a ceremony. A splash, a newsletter sheet, or a cookie wall that covers the visit button spends the 10 seconds on your needs. Put those where they do not cover the day.

## The first screen, specified

A workable first screen has three parts. A photograph of students in the day, cropped so the group and the work are visible. One sentence that names the age and a true limit or advantage. A way to visit or inquire, without a page transition you did not need.

The photograph should be the same truth as the wide lead, recomposed for a tall frame. If the honest crop loses the class, use a frame that was directed for the phone, not a slice the browser invented. Art direction is two crops, chosen on purpose. Neither crop is the crest.

The sentence should not be the mission. "Year 4 reads aloud in a group of about eighteen" is a first screen. "Inspiring tomorrow's thinkers" is a delay, and in small type it is an insult. You have room for very few words. Spend them on the fact that changes the comparison.

The control should be tappable at the bottom if you can place it there without covering the children entirely. A button that loads late and pushes the picture down is the layout shift web.dev asks you to avoid. Reserve the space. Then show the dates or the short form.

If a full inquiry is too tall, the first screen can hold the child's year and a continue action. Do not hold an essay. Do not hold ten fields. The job is to start a visit, not to complete a pupil record on the pavement.

## What the desktop spread steals

Desktop layouts steal the first view for atmosphere. A navigation bar of departments. A margin like a printed prospectus. A hero that is mostly lawn. When those choices are only narrowed, the phone gets leftovers: a menu icon, a cropped shield, and the visit link below the fold, under a mission line that wrapped into six unreadable rows.

Decide the phone's first screen as its own layout. The wide version can add the gate, a longer caption, and a second age. It should not add a different promise. The sentence about year 4 stays. The button words stay. You are art-directing two frames of one page, not writing two schools.

Watch for facts that exist only on the wide layout. A class size beside the hero on desktop and missing on the phone will be missed by the parent most likely to decide there. If it matters, it goes on the phone early. If it does not, delete it from both.

Hover is not a plan. Any detail that appears only when a pointer rests on a photograph will never appear for a thumb. Put it in the caption. The phone is the main case for this decision, not an extra.

## The visit control, under a thumb

The control has to be tappable. A delicate text link designed to look like print fails on a phone, and it fails more often for people with less precise touch. Give the control real height. Separate it from the menu so a miss does not open the foundation story instead of the dates.

The response has to be quick. Interaction to Next Paint at 200 milliseconds or less is the web.dev bar. A visit button that waits on a heavy script before it acknowledges a tap feels broken. Broken doors send people to the other tab. Load what the dates need. Delay the rest: a chat you do not staff, a film, a map tile of the whole city.

Show a full year beside the control, not in a toast at the top while the keyboard is open. "Year 3 open mornings are listed here" should be visible as the thumb arrives. If a year is full, say it in the same place. Do not let a parent complete a long inquiry to learn a fact you could have printed next to the button.

Keep the same words as the header. "Visit" should not become "Embark" on the phone. A parent who switches from a laptop to a phone in the same evening should not have to relearn the verb.

## Pictures, type, and jump

A tall hero without reserved space will shove the visit button off screen just as the parent reaches for it. Set the image dimensions. Do not inject a banner above the picture after load. Do not let a third-party bar push the students down so the mission line can slide in.

Type should not sit on the photograph unless the picture was composed for it and the contrast holds in daylight on the pavement. White type on a pale classroom disappears outdoors. Put the sentence on a solid ground if you cannot guarantee the frame. Clever type across children's faces is also a courtesy problem. Do not write slogans over a child's head.

Do not autoplay a film. It spends data, it covers the day, and it often starts with the crest. Offer a still. Let a person start a film if you truly have one that shows a lesson. Most parents will not, because they came to see whether a visit is possible.

Test with the system text size increased one step. If the first screen collapses into overlapping lines, the layout is too fragile. Fix it. Do not ask families to keep the default size so your prospectus proportions can survive.

## A pass on a real phone

Run the pass on a phone you did not design on, over a normal connection. Load the page cold. If the students arrive after you have already started to leave, you are outside a good largest paint, or close enough that extra scripts will push you over on a worse day. web.dev's 2.5 seconds is a useful line for that argument with a vendor who wants another plugin.

Complete a visit request with a thumb only. No pinching. Note every zoom, wait, or wrong tap. Each note is a change.

Then walk the fee page and the age page on the same phone. A clear homepage that leads to a fee table the width of a spreadsheet still loses. Stack the fees: year, what is included, what is not, visit. A sideways table is a desktop leftover, and parents will misread a number rather than wrestle it.

Ask one parent who is not on your board to find the end time of the day, or whichever limit you are proud of disclosing, with no help. If they cannot find it on the phone, it is not disclosed. Move it up. Small type is how limits hide. The mission line trained everyone to accept small type. Untrain them.

## After the screen works, the odd question remains

A working first screen will not answer every family. A move from abroad, a learning need, a year that is full, a question about the stair and a specific child. Those need a contact path that says what happens next, without a ten-field trap. [What the inquiry should ask, and what it should refuse](/blog/a-contact-path-for-an-independent-school) is the next piece. Read it after the phone pass. Most of those messages will be typed on the same phone, outside the same gate.

To see how a first screen can stay plain, look at [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). The test is dull and fair: a thumb, daylight, and a parent who still has two other schools open.
